content: I'm wondering if people might have tips for making projects that depend on Mathlib more resilient to changes introduced by new Mathlib and Lean versions? I know that using the output to simp? is one. Are there others?

A (dual) tip to have a better time with breaking changes when bumping mathlib is to use hopscotch to bisect failures, or even consider onboarding your project to downstream-reports if it's an actively maintained project.
Another small one: follow the deprecation warnings that you get already. Very soon (once you upgrade to the coming Lean release candidate?), these will come with try this: suggestions.
Using the output to simp? when the simp is the final tactic in a proof can actually make your project less resilient (because sometimes lemma names change)

For this reason, mathlib style is to not use simp only as the final tactic in a proof: https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/style.html#squeezing-simp-calls
This is not yet followed consistently in mathlib, but these occurrences slowly get fixed over time.

Michael Rothgang said:

This is not yet followed consistently in mathlib, but these occurrences slowly get fixed over time.

I think I tested this once and iirc there were really thousands of unsqueezed terminal simp calls.
Replacing them systematically would be quite easy to do.
Would a few large scale PRs fixing those (when it doesnt lead to slowdowns) be welcome?
Don't we prefer simp only to simp even as a terminal tactic, when simp is very slow and simp only is quicker?

Yes, many exceptions are for performance reasons. @Felix Pernegger If you'd like to get a report of these quickly, there is #36728 setup already to report the change in heartbeats. (I still want a linter for this, but closed because I now think a different design that would be okay to have on by default would be better)

Artie Khovanov said:

Using the output to simp? when the simp is the final tactic in a proof can actually make your project less resilient (because sometimes lemma names change)

One thing we do in Iris-Lean, when possible, is to try and extract out the results of these big simp calls (ie. using have or suffices) so that it can be proven with an unsqueezed simp. We also try to use calc for the same purpose.
I find that having enough types written down in a proof to reconstruct it helps a lot.
How does Mathlib get updated so quickly with each release? It seems to be updated before each Lean release?
It is updated continuously against each nightly build
By hand, or is there some kind of script or automation?
I just imagine that takes a long time?
Lots of both – humans only come in when the build fails
I see. Many hands make light work I guess?

Also, should I prefer looking for higher power tactics? I use tauto because I have a general idea what it does, and I don't think it looks for existing theorems, but I mostly avoid the rest because I don't really know what they are actually doing.
But maybe they are more resilient to changes?

Paige Thomas said:

How does Mathlib get updated so quickly with each release? It seems to be updated before each Lean release?

Maybe because PR author introducing breaking changes know how to fix incompatible existing codes, since they write the PR and know what was changed. And they have responsibility fixing them before PR merging. While downstream users has fewer knowledges about that.
